issue.title: Should refugees repay the support they got while waiting?
issue.question: When someone is granted refugee status, should they be made to repay what the state paid to support them while their claim was decided?
issue.summary: The Immigration and Asylum Bill was due back in the Commons for report stage on 18 November 2026, according to a newsletter dated 17 November (s1). The Refugee Council was asking supporters to back amendments that would remove the £10,000 charge on refugees who receive asylum support while their claim is considered (s1). The government says the Bill includes a new way to require asylum seekers in taxpayer-funded accommodation to contribute to costs when they can afford to (s2).

bench.title: Cap the refugee charge and tie it to ability to pay
bench.answer: Keep the Bill's contribution mechanism, which the government says applies to asylum seekers in taxpayer-funded accommodation who can afford to pay (s2), but replace the flat £10,000 charge on refugees (s1) with an income-tested contribution under a fixed cap. The Home Office would assess means at the point of grant and collect only from earnings. Free food, money and a bed would stay in place while a claim is decided. Amendments at report stage (s1) would set this in the Bill. It worked if repayments are collected without causing destitution, and if the Home Office publishes yearly collected sums against collection costs. Simulated citizens backed an ability-to-pay cap (27 backers) and a no-destitution limit (36).

bench.title: Take refugee repayment out of the Home Office's hands
bench.answer: Drop the flat £10,000 charge on refugees who received asylum support (s1). The government says the Bill lets it require asylum seekers in taxpayer-funded accommodation to contribute when they can afford to (s2). Give that affordability test to an independent assessor, not the department that runs the asylum system. Parliament fixes a cap; the assessor sets income-based amounts, publishes every decision, and collects only through tax once someone works. Success: no one left without money, food or a bed while waiting, which 36 simulated citizens backed as a limit, and published figures show how much is recovered against what collecting it costs.

bench.title: Drop the debt; put support under local control
bench.answer: In this simulation, Parliament should remove the £10,000 charge described in s1. Support while a claim is decided should not become a bill for gaining refugee status. Councils should fund local support groups steered jointly by refugees using the service and other local residents. Those groups should choose providers and publish spending, with no provider voting on its own contract. Central government should guarantee money for food and shelter, while residents steer delivery. Judge success after a year: lower costs per person, fewer people losing shelter, and no repayment debts from support received while waiting.

gate.verdict: No answer passes everything: each meets some tests and fails others, because the tests pull in opposite directions. Facts cannot settle whether refugees should repay at all, or how a taxpayer's bill weighs against a fresh start.

jury.question: Should refugees repay any of the support they got while waiting, or is that support simply part of running a fair asylum system?
options: No charge: support while waiting is the cost of a fair system
Repay only what they can afford, under a fixed cap
Repay through tax once they are working
Repay the full cost, whatever their income
jury.ruling: Repay only what they can afford, under a fixed cap. Four of 12 simulated jurors chose it, and it was the most common view in a split jury.

reasons.text: If they earn enough, fine, pay some back. But a limit, so it doesn't crush anyone starting out.
Support while waiting is part of a fair system. I would not bill people who fled.
The taxpayer paid, so they should pay it back. A mortgage is not optional for me either.
Take it from wages once they have a job, not before. Then they can stand up first.

minister.trial: In one simulated area, for six months, refugees granted status pay back support only from earnings, by an income test, under a fixed cap, with food, money and a bed kept in place while the claim is decided.
minister.fail_number: If more than 1 in 10 people in the trial fall behind on rent or go without food after paying, or the cost of collecting is above what is collected, it has failed.
minister.statement: Yes, it's a cost. The jury, twelve simulated jurors, split: three said drop it, four said repay what you can afford, two said repay through tax, three said repay it all. So we start with the middle. Pay back from earnings, by an income test, under a cap. Nobody goes without food or a bed while they wait. We count who falls behind and what collecting costs. If the cost of chasing is bigger than the money chased, we stop.
